name: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
problem: Open-domain QA retrieval used TF-IDF/BM25, which fails on semantic paraphrase and requires hand-tuned sparse statistics.
mechanism: A dual encoder (two independent BERT towers, no token-level interaction) maps a question and a passage to a single dense vector; retrieval is nearest-neighbour search over the passage index with a contrastive in-batch-negatives objective. Document embeddings are computed OFFLINE once per corpus; only the query needs an encoder pass at query time.
speedup_reported: Outperforms a strong Lucene-BM25 system by 9%-19% absolute top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on a range of open-domain QA datasets, and lifts end-to-end QA to new state of the art on multiple benchmarks. Baseline (Lucene-BM25) and metric (top-20 accuracy) are both stated; no hardware or latency disclosed.
notes:
Venue EMNLP 2020 (arXiv comment). DPR is the template for essentially every dense retriever since: separate encoders, in-batch negatives, offline document embedding. THE ARCHITECTURAL SERVING ARGUMENT: because documents are embedded OFFLINE, the serving cost of a dense index is (a) a one-time corpus embedding pass and (b) a query encoder forward plus an ANN scan - the expensive transformer never runs per document at query time. That asymmetry versus cross-encoders, which re-encode every candidate, is why dense retrieval won. The memory cost is the index, which is why dimensionality-reduction work (pap-mm-matryoshka) matters so much here.
